choices.text: The temperature difference is largest in winter, when heating systems run.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the difference is smallest in winter.

choices.text: Replacing pavement with vegetation would lower nighttime temperatures in the city.

stimulus.title: The Warm City
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The city center is about 4°C warmer at night than the surrounding farmland because of what the city is made of. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and store the heat, releasing it slowly after sunset. These surfaces are also dark, so they reflect less sunlight than fields and forests do. Vegetation cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, but the city has replaced most plants with pavement. The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights, when stored heat is released most effectively, and smallest in winter, when the sun is weak. Painting roofs white and planting trees would reduce the difference.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The warmth comes mainly from the energy people use. Every engine, air conditioner, furnace, and light releases heat into the city's air. In the dense center, this waste heat per square kilometer can rival the energy delivered by sunlight. The nighttime difference is large because the city keeps releasing heat after the sun sets, while the countryside does not. The difference also grows on weekdays, when traffic and business activity are heaviest, and shrinks on holidays, something that building materials alone cannot explain. Reducing energy use and improving the efficiency of vehicles and buildings would do more than changing roof colors.

stimulus.title: The Collapse at Carver Road
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The sudden hole that opened beneath Carver Road formed because rainwater slowly dissolved the limestone beneath the surface. Limestone is made of a mineral that dissolves in slightly acidic water, and rain becomes acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil. Over thousands of years, water seeping down through cracks widened them into a cavern. The roof of the cavern thinned until it could no longer hold up the road. Caves and springs are common in the surrounding countryside, and the hole has sheer walls of solid limestone, exactly as expected when a cavern roof gives way.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The hole formed because a leaking water main washed away the soil beneath the road. The main, installed sixty years ago, runs directly under the collapse and was found to be cracked. Escaping water carried fine soil particles into a nearby storm drain, leaving a growing void just below the pavement. Limestone caverns take thousands of years to form, but the road showed no sign of sinking until two months before the collapse, soon after water pressure in the main was raised. The hole's walls are mostly loose soil, and the solid rock lies several meters deeper. Repairing the main is the key to preventing another collapse.

stimulus.title: The Bleaching Reef
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The reef bleached because the water became too warm. Corals live with tiny algae inside their tissues that supply most of their food and give them their color. When water temperature stays more than about one degree above the summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down: the coral expels the algae and turns white. Satellite records show that the sea surface over the reef was unusually warm for six weeks before the bleaching, and the most heavily bleached patches were in shallow water, where the water warmed most. Reefs far from any town or farm bleached in the same weeks, which only a regional cause such as temperature can explain.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The main cause was runoff from the land. Heavy rains in the months before the bleaching carried soil, fertilizer, and sewage from the coast onto the reef. Sediment clouds the water and settles on the corals, smothering them, while nutrients feed seaweeds that overgrow the coral and bacteria that attack its tissue. Water samples near the river mouth showed nutrient levels several times higher than normal, and bleaching was most severe on the parts of the reef closest to the river. Warm water can stress corals, but these corals had survived warmer summers before. The difference this year was the condition of the water, not its temperature alone.

choices.rationale: Dependence on crowd size supports Scientist 1.

choices.text: The sway stopped shortly after the bridge was closed to pedestrians.
choices.rationale: Stopping when cleared supports Scientist 1.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's cause is the crowd; sway before the crowd arrived contradicts it.

stimulus.title: The Swaying Footbridge
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The bridge swayed from side to side on its opening day because of the people walking on it. When a crowd walks across a flexible bridge, small sideways movements make people adjust their steps to keep their balance. Many walkers end up stepping in time with the sway, and their combined footsteps push the bridge at exactly the frequency at which it naturally rocks. The more the bridge moves, the more people fall into step, so the motion grows. The sway appeared only when the crowd was large and stopped within minutes when the crowd was cleared, and no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The sway was caused by wind. As wind flows past the bridge deck and cables, it sheds swirling eddies alternately from each side, producing a push that switches direction at a regular rate. If that rate matches a natural frequency of the bridge, the structure rocks in resonance. The opening day was breezy, and the deck's flat shape is well suited to shedding eddies. Pedestrians certainly felt the motion and reacted to it, but their steps were a response to the sway, not its cause. Adding fins to the deck to break up the eddies, rather than limiting the crowd, is the correct fix.

questions.prompt: With which of the following statements would Scientist 2 most likely agree?

choices.text: The climate at the time the layer formed was far too warm for any glacier to exist.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says climate records show it was cold enough for ice.

choices.text: Flat-faced stones with parallel scratches indicate transport beneath moving ice.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 2 cites the scratched, flat-faced stones as evidence of dragging beneath ice.

choices.text: The unsorted bed beneath the pebbles was deposited by a slow-moving river.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says only ice can deposit such an unsorted mixture.

choices.text: Pebbles become well rounded only after long-distance transport in a river.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says pebbles can be rounded in meltwater streams over short distances.

questions.explanation: The scratched stones are one of Scientist 2's key pieces of evidence for ice.

stimulus.title: The Pebble Layer
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pebble layer exposed in the quarry wall was laid down by a fast-flowing river. The pebbles are well rounded, which happens when stones tumble against each other in moving water over long distances. They are sorted by size, with coarse pebbles at the bottom grading up to sand, exactly what a river deposits as its current slows. Many pebbles lie tilted in the same direction, the way a current stacks flat stones against the flow. The layer is also lens-shaped, thick in the middle and thinning to the sides, which matches the shape of a river channel cut into the older rock beneath it.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The layer was deposited by a glacier and the meltwater streams that flowed from it. Beneath the pebbles is a bed of unsorted material containing clay, sand, and boulders mixed together, a mixture that only ice can carry and drop in one place. Several of the larger stones have flat faces with parallel scratches, which form when stones are dragged along beneath moving ice. The pebbles above could have been rounded in meltwater streams at the glacier's edge, where sorting and tilting also occur over short distances. The region's climate records show it was cold enough for ice at the time, while river deposits need no such conditions.

questions.prompt: Both scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: sunlight was blocked for only a few days after the impact.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says sunlight was blocked for months; Scientist 2 does not discuss this.

choices.text: the asteroid struck before any groups of animals had begun to decline.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says some groups were already declining before the boundary formed.

choices.text: a clay layer rich in iridium marks the time of the extinction.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both refer to the iridium-rich boundary layer; they disagree only about where the iridium came from.

choices.text: volcanic gases alone were enough to change the climate.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 attributes the climate change to volcanic gases.

questions.explanation: The existence of the iridium layer at the boundary is accepted by both; its origin is what they dispute.

stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: Winter colonies in intact forest patches survived a severe storm that killed most butterflies in thinned patches nearby.
choices.rationale: Correct. Survival that depends on forest condition during a storm is exactly Scientist 2's mechanism.

choices.text: Milkweed counts on farmland fell by more than half over the same years as the monarch decline.
choices.rationale: This supports Scientist 1's milkweed explanation.

choices.text: Regions with abundant milkweed saw monarch declines as steep as regions with little milkweed.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 3's argument against Scientist 1.

choices.text: Caterpillars raised on milkweed collected from treated fields died at twice the rate of those raised on untreated plants.
choices.rationale: This supports Scientist 3's insecticide explanation.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2's claim is that forest thinning raises winter mortality; a storm that kills butterflies only in thinned patches demonstrates it.

stimulus.title: The Missing Monarchs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Monarch butterflies have declined because the plants their caterpillars eat are disappearing. Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed, which once grew between rows of corn and soybeans across the continent. Since farms began planting crops that tolerate weed killers, milkweed has been sprayed out of millions of hectares of farmland. Surveys show milkweed on farmland has fallen by more than half, and the decline in monarchs tracks the loss closely. Fewer plants mean fewer eggs laid and fewer caterpillars surviving to migrate. Restoring milkweed along roadsides and field edges is the most direct way to rebuild the population.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The decline is driven by what happens in winter. Nearly the entire population spends the cold months clustered in a few mountain forests, where dense fir trees shelter them from frost and rain. Illegal logging has thinned those forests, and butterflies in thinned stands freeze during winter storms at several times the rate of those in intact forest. Counts of the winter colonies show the sharpest drops in years with storms following logging. Even with plenty of milkweed, a population that loses most of its adults each winter cannot recover. Protecting the winter forests must come first.

Scientist 3
Neither milkweed loss nor logging explains the full pattern. Monarch numbers fell fastest in regions where milkweed was still common, and some years with mild winters still produced small spring populations. The missing factor is insecticide. Seeds coated with long-lasting insecticides are now planted on most cornfields, and the chemicals spread into nearby milkweed. Caterpillars that eat treated milkweed grow slowly and die at higher rates, and adults exposed to the chemicals lay fewer eggs. The decline began within a few years of the coated seeds coming into wide use, which neither of the other explanations accounts for.

questions.prompt: Suppose a new analysis showed that the water-bearing minerals on Mars formed from water that was already present in the volcanic rock when it erupted, not from surface water. This finding would most likely:

choices.rationale: Correct. If the minerals did not absorb surface water, they cannot be where the rivers' water went.
The finding does not concern escape to space.
The finding removes the link between the minerals and the lost surface water.
The finding bears only on Scientist 2's reservoir.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2's reservoir only explains the missing rivers if the minerals absorbed surface water; the finding breaks that link.

stimulus.title: Where Mars's Water Went
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Mars once had rivers and lakes, and most of that water escaped to space. Early in its history Mars lost its global magnetic field, which had shielded the atmosphere from the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. Without that shield, the particles stripped gas from the top of the atmosphere, and the planet's weak gravity could not hold it back. As the air thinned, surface water boiled or froze, and water vapor rising into the upper atmosphere was broken apart by sunlight, with the light hydrogen escaping. A spacecraft orbiting Mars today still measures hydrogen and oxygen leaking away, and the ratio of heavy to light hydrogen in the remaining water shows that most of the original water is gone.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Most of the water never left; it is locked inside the crust. When water reacts with volcanic rock, it becomes part of the minerals that form, such as clays. Orbiting instruments have found such water-bearing minerals across large areas of the Martian surface, and rovers have measured water bound in the rocks they drill. Calculations of how much water those minerals can hold suggest that the crust could contain an ocean's worth. Escape to space is real but slow, and at the rates measured today it cannot account for the amount of water the early rivers required. Mars dried out mainly because its water was absorbed by the ground.

choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 blames the quantity of milkweed; Scientist 3 blames insecticide contamination of the milkweed that remains.

choices.text: whether monarch butterflies migrate each autumn to the same few mountain forests.
choices.rationale: Neither disputes the migration.

choices.text: whether coated seeds are planted on most cornfields.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not dispute how seeds are planted.

questions.prompt: Which of the following discoveries, if made, would most seriously undermine Scientist 1's explanation?

choices.text: Records show the water over the reef never exceeded the summer maximum during the bleaching year.
choices.rationale: Correct. Without the prolonged warmth, Scientist 1's cause is absent.

choices.text: Water samples taken near the river mouth contain nutrient levels several times higher than normal.
choices.rationale: Nutrient levels concern Scientist 2's view and do not undercut the temperature claim.

choices.text: Shallow corals bleached more severely than deeper corals.
choices.rationale: Shallow water warming most fits Scientist 1's view.

choices.text: Reefs far from the coast bleached during the same weeks.
choices.rationale: Distant reefs bleaching is Scientist 1's own evidence.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's explanation requires water staying above the summer maximum; records showing it never did remove that cause.

stimulus.title: The Bleaching Reef
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The reef bleached because the water became too warm. Corals live with tiny algae inside their tissues that supply most of their food and give them their color. When water temperature stays more than about one degree above the summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down: the coral expels the algae and turns white. Satellite records show that the sea surface over the reef was unusually warm for six weeks before the bleaching, and the most heavily bleached patches were in shallow water, where the water warmed most. Reefs far from any town or farm bleached in the same weeks, which only a regional cause such as temperature can explain.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The main cause was runoff from the land. Heavy rains in the months before the bleaching carried soil, fertilizer, and sewage from the coast onto the reef. Sediment clouds the water and settles on the corals, smothering them, while nutrients feed seaweeds that overgrow the coral and bacteria that attack its tissue. Water samples near the river mouth showed nutrient levels several times higher than normal, and bleaching was most severe on the parts of the reef closest to the river. Warm water can stress corals, but these corals had survived warmer summers before. The difference this year was the condition of the water, not its temperature alone.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims is most consistent with Scientist 1's viewpoint?

choices.text: Pines on the well-watered lower slopes resist beetles because they make more resin.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's explanation.

choices.text: Thinning the stand to reduce competition for water would save the remaining trees.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's recommendation.

choices.text: Warmer winters have allowed more beetles to survive and reproduce.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 attributes the beetle surge to warm winters.

choices.text: Trees on the ridge were growing poorly for years before the beetles arrived.
choices.rationale: The tree-ring evidence belongs to Scientist 2.

questions.explanation: The link between warm winters and beetle numbers is Scientist 1's explanation for the outbreak.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

questions.prompt: Despite their disagreement, both scientists would accept that:

choices.text: a leaf's autumn color provides no benefit at all to the tree.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 argues that red color is beneficial.

choices.text: the tree makes new pigments in its leaves as autumn begins.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the colors are revealed, not made.

choices.text: red pigments protect the cells of a leaf from excess light.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 makes this claim.

choices.text: yellow pigments are present in leaves before autumn begins.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says yellow pigments are present all along; Scientist 2 concedes yellow may be unmasked.

questions.explanation: Both allow that yellow is unmasked; the dispute is over red.

stimulus.title: The Colors of Autumn
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The red and yellow colors of autumn leaves are simply revealed, not made. Throughout summer a leaf is packed with green chlorophyll, which hides yellow and orange pigments that are present all along and help capture light. As days shorten, the tree stops repairing chlorophyll and breaks it down to recover its nitrogen, and the green fades. The yellow pigments remain and finally show. Red colors come from the breakdown of sugars trapped in the leaf once the tree seals off the leaf stem. The display is a side effect of recycling, which is why a leaf's color has no clear benefit to the tree.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Red autumn leaves are produced on purpose. The red pigments, called anthocyanins, are not present in summer; the leaf makes them fresh in autumn, using energy and sugar at a time when the tree is shutting down. Making them would be wasteful unless they did something useful. Anthocyanins absorb excess light and protect the leaf's cells while the tree pulls valuable nutrients out of the leaf before it drops. Leaves on the sunny side of a tree turn redder than shaded leaves, and trees growing in poor soil, which need to recover nutrients most, produce the reddest leaves. Yellow pigments may be unmasked, but red is manufactured.

questions.prompt: Suppose researchers removed all magnetite from a group of bees and found that, on sunny days, these bees returned to the hive from unfamiliar locations just as well as untreated bees. This finding would most likely:

choices.rationale: Losing magnetite without losing navigation argues against the magnetic explanation.
The finding favors the sun-compass view.
Normal navigation on sunny days is what the sun-compass view predicts.
Correct. If bees navigate normally without magnetite, the magnetic sense cannot be their main guide, at least when the sun is available.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2 makes magnetite the key sensor; bees that navigate without it undercut that claim.

stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.

questions.prompt: Which of the following discoveries, if made, would most seriously undermine Scientist 1's explanation?

choices.text: Plankton in a tank migrate on the same schedule with or without fish, as long as the deep water is colder.
choices.rationale: Correct. Migration that ignores the presence of fish but tracks temperature contradicts predator avoidance.

choices.text: Fish that eat plankton hunt by sight and feed mostly during daylight.
choices.rationale: Visual daytime predators fit Scientist 1's view.

choices.text: The daily migration is strongest in clear lakes where sunlight penetrates deeply.
choices.rationale: Deeper light penetration means greater exposure, consistent with Scientist 1.

choices.text: Plankton that remain at the surface all day are eaten at a much higher rate than those that migrate downward.
choices.rationale: Higher predation at the surface supports Scientist 1.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's mechanism predicts a response to predators; migration unchanged by their absence undercuts it.

stimulus.title: The Nightly Rise of Plankton
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Tiny animals called zooplankton spend the day hundreds of meters below the surface and rise to feed near the top only after dark because they are hiding from predators. The fish that eat them hunt by sight, so a plankton animal near the sunlit surface in daytime is easily seen and eaten. In the dark depths it is nearly invisible. Experiments in large tanks show that plankton stay deeper when fish are present and rise earlier when fish are removed, even if the light is unchanged. In lakes with no fish, the daily migration is weak or absent. The pattern is a trade-off: the surface offers food, but only the night makes it safe.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The migration is a way of saving energy. Water near the surface is warm, and a cold-blooded animal's body uses up energy faster in warm water. By feeding briefly at the surface and then sinking into cold, deep water, a plankton animal digests its food while burning fuel slowly, so it grows faster on the same amount of food. Measurements show that plankton which migrate convert food into body mass more efficiently than those that remain at the surface. Predators may matter in some lakes, but the migration also occurs in the open ocean where visual predators are scarce, and it follows the daily cycle of light because light sets the animals' internal clock, not because light reveals them.

questions.prompt: Scientist 2 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

stimulus.title: Methane Over the Marsh
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The methane detected over the marsh comes from microbes in the waterlogged soil. In mud with no oxygen, certain microbes break down dead plant material and release methane as a waste product, and the gas bubbles up through the water. Methane levels over the marsh rise in late summer, when the mud is warmest and the microbes are most active, and fall in winter. Samples of gas from bubbles in the mud have the chemical signature typical of microbial methane, with very little of the heavier gases found in natural gas. The marsh releases more methane per hectare than nearby forest or farmland, as wetlands do throughout the world.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The excess methane comes from an aging natural-gas pipeline that crosses the marsh. The highest methane readings are concentrated in a narrow band along the pipeline route rather than spread evenly across the marsh, and they do not fall off in winter the way microbial emissions would. Gas collected directly above the pipeline contains ethane and propane, which microbes do not produce. Microbial methane is real, but it was present long before monitoring began, while the excess appeared only after the pipeline's pressure was raised. Repairing the pipeline would remove most of the signal.

Scientist 3
A third source has been overlooked: ancient methane trapped in a layer of frozen ground beneath the marsh. The frozen layer has been thawing from below as the climate warms, releasing gas that formed thousands of years ago. This old methane contains almost no radioactive carbon, unlike the fresh methane that microbes make from recently living plants. Measurements of the marsh air show a methane mixture that is older than microbial gas alone could explain. Thaw releases are steady year-round and strongest where the frozen layer is thinnest, which happens to be near the pipeline route, so the pipeline has been blamed for a signal it did not create.

stimulus.title: The Perch of Miller Lake
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The decline of perch in Miller Lake began soon after the farms upstream expanded. Fertilizer washed into the lake by rain feeds algae, which bloom across the surface each summer. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Measurements taken in August show oxygen levels near the bottom of the lake that are too low for perch eggs and young fish to survive. Adult perch can move to shallower water, but their young cannot, so each year fewer fish reach adulthood. Reducing fertilizer runoff would allow the oxygen to recover and the perch population to rebuild.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The perch decline is due to the arrival of the zander, a predatory fish first recorded in Miller Lake eight years ago, probably released by anglers. Zander feed heavily on young perch, and their numbers have grown each year while the perch count has fallen. Low oxygen alone cannot explain the pattern: the lake had algae blooms for decades before perch began to decline, and nearby lakes with similar farms and blooms still have healthy perch populations but no zander. Stomach samples from zander in the lake contain mostly young perch. Removing zander by netting would allow the perch to recover even if the fertilizer runoff continued.

stimulus.title: The Vanishing Frogs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Frog populations in mountain streams across the region have crashed because of a fungus that infects amphibian skin. Frogs breathe and take in water partly through their skin, and the infection disrupts this exchange until the heart fails. The fungus has been found on dead frogs at every site where populations collapsed, and healthy populations remain only where the fungus is absent. Declines have spread from valley to valley in a wave, the way a contagious disease spreads, and have hit protected parks with clean water as hard as farmland. Frogs raised in captivity and exposed to the fungus die within weeks.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The declines are the result of pesticides carried by wind and rain from farms into the mountains. Pesticide residues have been measured in stream water, in frog tissue, and even in snow at high elevations. These chemicals weaken the frogs' immune systems, which is why a fungus that frogs have lived with for a long time now kills them. The fungus is found on many healthy frogs in regions with little agriculture, so its presence alone does not cause collapse. Declines are also most severe at sites downwind of major farming areas. Reducing pesticide drift would let the frogs resist the fungus as they once did.

questions.prompt: The two viewpoints differ mainly on which of the following points?

choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 describes a sudden impact; Scientist 2 describes eruptions lasting hundreds of thousands of years.

choices.text: Whether the clay layer at the boundary actually contains the element iridium.
choices.rationale: Both accept the iridium layer and differ only on its source.

choices.text: Whether the global climate was seriously disrupted at the time of the extinction.

stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

choices.text: trees that die of drought show no sign of beetle damage.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the dead trees were attacked by beetles.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

choices.text: Milkweed has disappeared from most of the farmland where it once grew.

stimulus.title: The Missing Monarchs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Monarch butterflies have declined because the plants their caterpillars eat are disappearing. Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed, which once grew between rows of corn and soybeans across the continent. Since farms began planting crops that tolerate weed killers, milkweed has been sprayed out of millions of hectares of farmland. Surveys show milkweed on farmland has fallen by more than half, and the decline in monarchs tracks the loss closely. Fewer plants mean fewer eggs laid and fewer caterpillars surviving to migrate. Restoring milkweed along roadsides and field edges is the most direct way to rebuild the population.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The decline is driven by what happens in winter. Nearly the entire population spends the cold months clustered in a few mountain forests, where dense fir trees shelter them from frost and rain. Illegal logging has thinned those forests, and butterflies in thinned stands freeze during winter storms at several times the rate of those in intact forest. Counts of the winter colonies show the sharpest drops in years with storms following logging. Even with plenty of milkweed, a population that loses most of its adults each winter cannot recover. Protecting the winter forests must come first.

Scientist 3
Neither milkweed loss nor logging explains the full pattern. Monarch numbers fell fastest in regions where milkweed was still common, and some years with mild winters still produced small spring populations. The missing factor is insecticide. Seeds coated with long-lasting insecticides are now planted on most cornfields, and the chemicals spread into nearby milkweed. Caterpillars that eat treated milkweed grow slowly and die at higher rates, and adults exposed to the chemicals lay fewer eggs. The decline began within a few years of the coated seeds coming into wide use, which neither of the other explanations accounts for.

questions.prompt: With which of the following statements would Scientist 1 most likely agree?

choices.text: The Moon's small core simply reflects the composition it had when it formed elsewhere.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 explains the small core as a result of the impact stripping Earth's rocky exterior.

choices.text: The Moon is made mostly of material that once belonged to Earth's outer layers.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says the collision blasted rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit to form the Moon.

choices.text: The matching oxygen isotopes are a coincidence of where the Moon formed.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 offers this explanation; Scientist 1 attributes the match to a shared origin in the impact.

choices.text: The Moon formed far from Earth and was captured by Earth's gravity later on.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's capture view.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's model builds the Moon out of Earth's outer material.

stimulus.title: The Origin of the Moon
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision blasted molten rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it quickly gathered into the Moon. This explains why the Moon's rocks match Earth's in the ratios of oxygen isotopes, which differ from one body to another in the solar system. It also explains why the Moon has a very small iron core: the impact stripped mostly rocky material from the outside of the Earth, leaving Earth's iron core behind. The Moon's rocks are also unusually dry, as expected if they were once heated enough to drive off their water.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was captured by Earth's gravity as it passed nearby. Capture explains why the Moon is so large compared with Earth; the impact scenario should have left a much smaller moon or none at all, as computer models of similar collisions often show. The matching oxygen isotopes could result from the Moon forming in the same region of the solar system as Earth, from the same raw material. A capture would have left the Moon in a tilted orbit, and the Moon's orbit is indeed tilted relative to Earth's equator. The small core could simply reflect the Moon's original composition.

choices.rationale: Correct. Both passages begin from the early rivers and lakes.

stimulus.title: Where Mars's Water Went
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Mars once had rivers and lakes, and most of that water escaped to space. Early in its history Mars lost its global magnetic field, which had shielded the atmosphere from the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. Without that shield, the particles stripped gas from the top of the atmosphere, and the planet's weak gravity could not hold it back. As the air thinned, surface water boiled or froze, and water vapor rising into the upper atmosphere was broken apart by sunlight, with the light hydrogen escaping. A spacecraft orbiting Mars today still measures hydrogen and oxygen leaking away, and the ratio of heavy to light hydrogen in the remaining water shows that most of the original water is gone.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Most of the water never left; it is locked inside the crust. When water reacts with volcanic rock, it becomes part of the minerals that form, such as clays. Orbiting instruments have found such water-bearing minerals across large areas of the Martian surface, and rovers have measured water bound in the rocks they drill. Calculations of how much water those minerals can hold suggest that the crust could contain an ocean's worth. Escape to space is real but slow, and at the rates measured today it cannot account for the amount of water the early rivers required. Mars dried out mainly because its water was absorbed by the ground.

questions.prompt: Suppose new dating showed that the drought began fifty years after the city's population had already fallen by half. This finding would most likely:

stimulus.title: Why the City Was Abandoned
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The ancient city was abandoned because of a long drought. Layers of lake sediment from the region show a sharp drop in rainfall lasting more than a century, beginning just before the city's population began to fall. The city depended on reservoirs filled by seasonal rains, and excavations show the reservoirs were enlarged twice late in the city's history, a sign that water was becoming scarce. Tree-ring records from the surrounding hills confirm several decades of poor growth in the same period. Without reliable water, crops failed, and the people left for river valleys where farming remained possible.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The city was undone by its own irrigation. For centuries farmers watered their fields from canals, and in a hot climate much of that water evaporated, leaving behind the salts it carried. Soil samples from the old fields contain salt levels far too high for wheat, the city's main crop, and pollen records show a late shift toward barley, which tolerates salt better. Written tablets from the final decades record shrinking harvests on fields that still received water. A drought may have added to the strain, but the fields were already failing from salt before the dry period, and no amount of rain would have washed it away quickly.

choices.text: whether plankton are able to swim up and down through the water column.

choices.text: whether plankton migrate to avoid being eaten or to save energy.

choices.text: whether light levels change over the course of a day.

stimulus.title: The Nightly Rise of Plankton
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Tiny animals called zooplankton spend the day hundreds of meters below the surface and rise to feed near the top only after dark because they are hiding from predators. The fish that eat them hunt by sight, so a plankton animal near the sunlit surface in daytime is easily seen and eaten. In the dark depths it is nearly invisible. Experiments in large tanks show that plankton stay deeper when fish are present and rise earlier when fish are removed, even if the light is unchanged. In lakes with no fish, the daily migration is weak or absent. The pattern is a trade-off: the surface offers food, but only the night makes it safe.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The migration is a way of saving energy. Water near the surface is warm, and a cold-blooded animal's body uses up energy faster in warm water. By feeding briefly at the surface and then sinking into cold, deep water, a plankton animal digests its food while burning fuel slowly, so it grows faster on the same amount of food. Measurements show that plankton which migrate convert food into body mass more efficiently than those that remain at the surface. Predators may matter in some lakes, but the migration also occurs in the open ocean where visual predators are scarce, and it follows the daily cycle of light because light sets the animals' internal clock, not because light reveals them.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken Scientist 1's viewpoint?

choices.text: Bees whose view of the sky is blocked by a cap return home as reliably as bees with a clear view.
choices.rationale: Correct. If blocking the sky does not impair homing, the sky cannot be the main cue.

choices.text: Bees often fail to return on days with no polarized light in the sky.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: Bees held in the dark for several hours fly off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: Bees communicate the direction of food relative to the sun.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 1's own evidence.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's view requires the sky; normal navigation without it undermines the view.

stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.

questions.prompt:
[Fed twice a day], the goats grew fat by spring.

What is the best way to write the bracketed portion? (Choose NO CHANGE if it is best as written.)

choices.rationale: Correct. The bracketed wording is already right: 'Fed twice a day' describes 'the goats', the noun that follows the comma.

choices.text: The farmer fed them twice a day
choices.rationale: This is an independent clause, so a comma alone creates a comma splice.

choices.text: Being fed by the farmer twice a day by him
choices.rationale: This phrase does not describe 'the goats'; it dangles.

choices.text: With twice-daily feedings from the farmer
choices.rationale: This version is wordy and still fails to modify the subject that follows.

questions.explanation: The phrase before the comma must describe the subject that follows it ('the goats'), and it must be a phrase, not a complete clause.

stimulus.title: Natural Science: The Bacterial Chorus
stimulus.text:
For much of the twentieth century, bacteria were regarded as the ultimate loners. Each cell, according to the prevailing view, went about its business independently, absorbing nutrients, dividing, and responding to its surroundings without any regard for its neighbors. A colony of bacteria was simply a crowd of individuals that happened to be in the same place. That picture has changed dramatically. Researchers now know that many bacteria communicate with chemicals, and that by doing so they can act together in ways no single cell could manage.

Some of the earliest clues came from a glowing marine bacterium now called Vibrio fischeri. In laboratory cultures, scientists noticed something odd: when the bacteria were sparse, they produced no light at all, but when the population grew dense, the entire culture began to glow, more or less at once. Individual cells were clearly capable of producing light. Why would they wait until there were many of them to do it?

The answer turned out to involve a small molecule that each cell releases into its surroundings. When only a few bacteria are present, the molecule drifts away and its concentration stays low. As the population grows, more cells release more of the molecule, and its concentration rises. Once it passes a certain threshold, it triggers a change inside every cell: genes that had been switched off are switched on, and the cells begin to produce light. Because the signal reflects how many cells are nearby, researchers named the phenomenon quorum sensing, borrowing a term for the minimum number of members a group needs before it can make decisions.

Quorum sensing makes sense of a behavior that would otherwise seem wasteful. Producing light requires a great deal of energy. A single bacterium glowing in the open ocean would spend that energy for nothing, since its light would be far too faint to matter. But billions of bacteria glowing together can produce light bright enough to have an effect, and in the case of V. fischeri, that effect is put to use by an animal. The bacteria live inside a special organ of a small squid found in shallow Hawaiian waters. At night, the squid hunts near the surface, where moonlight from above would ordinarily cast its shadow downward, revealing it to predators below. The light produced by its bacterial partners is thought to cancel that shadow, helping to hide the squid. In return, the bacteria receive a protected, nutrient-rich home where they can reach the dense populations that switch on their glow.

Since the discovery of quorum sensing in light-producing bacteria, researchers have found that the strategy is remarkably widespread. Many bacteria use chemical signals to coordinate activities that pay off only when performed by large numbers of cells. Some disease-causing bacteria, for instance, appear to hold back the production of harmful substances until their numbers are large enough to overwhelm a host's defenses. Acting too early, when the population is small, might simply alert the immune system without accomplishing much.

That observation has opened an intriguing possibility for medicine. Most antibiotics work by killing bacteria or stopping their growth, and bacteria that survive a treatment can pass on whatever traits helped them survive, which over time produces resistant strains. Some researchers have proposed a different approach: rather than killing bacteria, interfere with their signals. If the bacteria never detect that they have reached a quorum, they may never launch the coordinated behaviors that make them dangerous. Because such a treatment would not directly threaten the bacteria's survival, some scientists have suggested that resistance might develop more slowly, though whether that hope will hold up in practice remains an open question.

Whatever its medical future, quorum sensing has changed how biologists think about the smallest forms of life. The notion of bacteria as solitary individuals has given way to a picture of populations that monitor, signal, and respond to one another. Even the simplest organisms, it turns out, may be listening to their neighbors.

stimulus.title: Natural Science: Bringing Back the Mammoth?
stimulus.text:
For most of history, extinction has meant forever. When the last member of a species died, everything that species was, including its behavior, its role in its ecosystem, and the genetic code that built it, was gone. Advances in genetics have begun to raise a startling possibility: that some lost species, or at least close approximations of them, might be brought back.

The leading approaches do not involve resurrecting an extinct animal in any literal sense. Instead, researchers recover fragments of DNA from preserved remains, compare them with the genomes of the extinct species' closest living relatives, and then edit the relatives' DNA to carry some of the traits that made the lost species distinctive. A project aimed at the woolly mammoth, for example, would produce an elephant engineered to have a mammoth's dense hair, thick fat, and tolerance for cold. The result would not be a mammoth in the full sense, but it might live where mammoths once lived and do some of what they once did.

Supporters argue that such work could do more than satisfy curiosity. Some extinct animals played important roles in their ecosystems. Large grazers, for instance, may once have helped maintain open grasslands in the far north by trampling snow and knocking down trees, and some scientists have suggested that restoring such grazing could help keep frozen soils from thawing. Bringing back a lost species, or a functional substitute for it, might in such cases help restore a damaged landscape.

The techniques developed along the way could also help species that are not yet extinct. Many endangered animals survive in populations so small that they have lost much of their genetic diversity, leaving them vulnerable to disease. The same tools used to edit traits into an elephant's genome might one day be used to restore lost diversity to a struggling population, using DNA preserved in museum specimens. Seen this way, de-extinction research is less a rival to conservation than a new set of instruments for it.

Finally, there is the matter of responsibility. Human activity drove many species to extinction. If we develop the means to undo some of that damage, it is worth asking whether we have an obligation to try.
stimulus.text_b:
The prospect of seeing a mammoth, or something like one, walk across the tundra is undeniably thrilling. But thrill is not the same as wisdom, and the case for de-extinction looks weaker the more closely it is examined.

Consider first what would actually be produced. An elephant edited to carry some mammoth traits is not a mammoth. It would lack the knowledge that real mammoths passed from one generation to the next, such as where to find food in winter and how to avoid predators, because there would be no mammoths left to teach it. It would be raised by elephants or by people, in a world whose climate, plants, and other animals have changed enormously over thousands of years. Whether such an animal could thrive, or would even fill the ecological role its supporters imagine, is far from clear.

Consider next the cost. Conservation budgets are small, and every dollar and every hour of expert attention spent on reviving a lost species is unavailable for protecting a living one. Thousands of species are threatened right now by habitat loss, pollution, and climate change, and many could be saved with measures that are already understood: protecting land, restoring wetlands, regulating hunting. These measures are rarely dramatic, which is perhaps why they struggle to attract attention. Even the most successful revival would produce, at enormous expense, a handful of animals; protecting a single stretch of habitat can shelter thousands.

There is also a subtler danger. If people come to believe that extinction can be reversed, they may take it less seriously. A developer weighing whether to clear a forest, or a government deciding whether to fund a wildlife refuge, might reason that a lost species could always be brought back later. Even if no scientist makes such a promise, the mere idea could weaken the urgency that conservation depends on.

None of this means that genetic research has nothing to offer. Tools for studying and even restoring genetic diversity in endangered populations may prove valuable. But that work can be pursued directly, for the sake of living species, without the spectacle of resurrection.

stimulus.title: Social Science: The Paths People Choose
stimulus.text:
Walk across almost any college campus or city park and you will find them: narrow ribbons of bare earth cutting diagonally across the grass, worn smooth by thousands of shoes. Landscape architects call them desire paths. They appear wherever the route people want to take differs from the route a designer has paved for them, and they are, in their quiet way, a form of protest. Each one records a small decision made again and again by people who will never meet: the paved path goes around, but I am going through.

For a long time, the standard response to desire paths was to fight them. Groundskeepers put up fences, planted hedges, and posted signs asking pedestrians to keep off the grass. These measures rarely worked for long. A sign can be ignored, and a hedge, sooner or later, develops a gap exactly the width of a person. The trouble was not that people were careless. It was that the paved paths had been laid out according to what looked orderly on a drawing, with neat right angles and symmetrical loops, rather than according to where people actually needed to go.

Some designers began to wonder whether the paths might be useful rather than merely annoying. If thousands of people independently chose the same shortcut, perhaps they were collectively solving a problem the designers had missed. A few universities have taken this idea to its logical conclusion. Rather than paving walkways when a new building opens, they plant the surrounding area with grass and wait. Over a season or two, students wear their own routes into the lawn. Only then do the planners pour concrete, following the lines the walkers have drawn. The result can look a little unusual from above, with walkways that branch at odd angles, but the grass on either side stays green because no one has a reason to leave the path.

The approach has an obvious appeal. It costs little, it produces paths that people will actually use, and it treats pedestrians as experts in their own movement. It also reflects a broader shift in how planners think about public space. Older approaches often began with a fixed vision and expected people to conform to it. Newer ones are more likely to start by observing behavior, such as counting foot traffic, watching where people pause, and noticing which benches go unused, and to treat that behavior as evidence rather than as a problem to be corrected.

Still, desire paths are not always a reliable guide. A shortcut that saves a few seconds on a dry afternoon may become a mud slide in the spring, and a route that suits students in a hurry may be too steep or uneven for someone using a wheelchair or pushing a stroller. Some paths form simply because one person cut a corner and others followed the visible trail, not because the route was especially efficient. In those cases, the path records habit more than need.

There is also the question of what gets lost. A lawn crisscrossed with paths is a lawn with less grass, and in some places the ground being worn away is not ornamental turf but fragile habitat. In national parks, rangers work hard to keep visitors on marked trails precisely because shortcuts can erode hillsides and damage plants that take decades to recover. What counts as a sensible shortcut in a city park may be a scar in a wilderness.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of desire paths, then, is not that the crowd is always right but that the crowd is always communicating. A worn strip of earth is information. It tells designers where their plans and people's needs have come apart. Sometimes the right response is to pave the path; sometimes it is to make the official route more appealing; occasionally it is to put up the fence after all. But ignoring the message entirely is rarely the right choice.

stimulus.title: Social Science: The Paths People Choose
stimulus.text:
Walk across almost any college campus or city park and you will find them: narrow ribbons of bare earth cutting diagonally across the grass, worn smooth by thousands of shoes. Landscape architects call them desire paths. They appear wherever the route people want to take differs from the route a designer has paved for them, and they are, in their quiet way, a form of protest. Each one records a small decision made again and again by people who will never meet: the paved path goes around, but I am going through.

For a long time, the standard response to desire paths was to fight them. Groundskeepers put up fences, planted hedges, and posted signs asking pedestrians to keep off the grass. These measures rarely worked for long. A sign can be ignored, and a hedge, sooner or later, develops a gap exactly the width of a person. The trouble was not that people were careless. It was that the paved paths had been laid out according to what looked orderly on a drawing, with neat right angles and symmetrical loops, rather than according to where people actually needed to go.

Some designers began to wonder whether the paths might be useful rather than merely annoying. If thousands of people independently chose the same shortcut, perhaps they were collectively solving a problem the designers had missed. A few universities have taken this idea to its logical conclusion. Rather than paving walkways when a new building opens, they plant the surrounding area with grass and wait. Over a season or two, students wear their own routes into the lawn. Only then do the planners pour concrete, following the lines the walkers have drawn. The result can look a little unusual from above, with walkways that branch at odd angles, but the grass on either side stays green because no one has a reason to leave the path.

The approach has an obvious appeal. It costs little, it produces paths that people will actually use, and it treats pedestrians as experts in their own movement. It also reflects a broader shift in how planners think about public space. Older approaches often began with a fixed vision and expected people to conform to it. Newer ones are more likely to start by observing behavior, such as counting foot traffic, watching where people pause, and noticing which benches go unused, and to treat that behavior as evidence rather than as a problem to be corrected.

Still, desire paths are not always a reliable guide. A shortcut that saves a few seconds on a dry afternoon may become a mud slide in the spring, and a route that suits students in a hurry may be too steep or uneven for someone using a wheelchair or pushing a stroller. Some paths form simply because one person cut a corner and others followed the visible trail, not because the route was especially efficient. In those cases, the path records habit more than need.

There is also the question of what gets lost. A lawn crisscrossed with paths is a lawn with less grass, and in some places the ground being worn away is not ornamental turf but fragile habitat. In national parks, rangers work hard to keep visitors on marked trails precisely because shortcuts can erode hillsides and damage plants that take decades to recover. What counts as a sensible shortcut in a city park may be a scar in a wilderness.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of desire paths, then, is not that the crowd is always right but that the crowd is always communicating. A worn strip of earth is information. It tells designers where their plans and people's needs have come apart. Sometimes the right response is to pave the path; sometimes it is to make the official route more appealing; occasionally it is to put up the fence after all. But ignoring the message entirely is rarely the right choice.

stimulus.title: Social Science: Keeping a Language Alive
stimulus.text:
When linguists speak of a language as endangered, they rarely mean that its words are disappearing from dictionaries. Dictionaries, after all, can preserve a language indefinitely, in the way a museum preserves a fossil. What linguists mean is that fewer and fewer children are learning it at home. A language can have tens of thousands of speakers and still be in danger if almost all of those speakers are grandparents; it can have only a few hundred and be relatively secure if those few hundred include toddlers. The crucial measure is not size but transmission: whether the language is being handed from one generation to the next.

Transmission tends to break down for reasons that have little to do with the language itself. When a family moves to a city, when schools teach in a single national language, when jobs and opportunity seem to require a different tongue, parents often make a reasonable calculation: their children will be better served by the language of power. Sometimes the calculation is forced on them. In many countries, children were punished in school for speaking their home language well into the twentieth century, and the shame attached to that punishment could last long after the policy ended.

Efforts to reverse this process, known as language revitalization, have multiplied in recent decades, and they have taught advocates some uncomfortable lessons. The first is that documentation, however valuable, is not the same as revival. Recording elderly speakers, compiling grammars, and archiving stories can preserve an extraordinary amount of knowledge, and these materials are often indispensable to later learners. But a language that exists only in recordings is, in an important sense, no longer being used to do anything: to argue, to joke, to comfort a child at night.

The second lesson is that classroom instruction alone rarely produces fluent speakers. A child who studies a heritage language for an hour a day, then spends the rest of the day in the dominant language, may learn a great deal about it without ever coming to think in it. For this reason, some of the most closely watched programs are immersion programs, in which young children spend the entire school day, and sometimes much of their home life, in the language being revived. The approach demands enormous resources: teachers who are fluent, materials that must often be written from scratch, and families willing to commit to it.

A third lesson concerns what counts as success. Revitalized languages almost always change. New learners, many of whom grew up speaking another language first, bring with them sounds, idioms, and patterns of grammar from that language. Elders sometimes find the speech of younger speakers jarring, even incorrect. Linguists who study these situations tend to be less troubled. Every living language changes, they point out, and a language spoken imperfectly by children is in a far stronger position than one spoken perfectly by no one.

This view is not universally shared, and the disagreement is not merely academic. For some communities, the purpose of revitalization is to recover a connection with ancestors, and a language that has drifted far from the speech of those ancestors may feel like a loss disguised as a gain. For others, the purpose is to give the language a future, and change is the price of that future. Both positions reflect real values, and the programs that seem to last are often those that make room for both, treating elders as the keepers of an authoritative tradition while allowing young speakers to make the language their own.

What revitalization cannot do is simply restore the past. A language that returns from the edge of disappearance returns into a different world from the one it left. That may be the most important lesson of all: a revived language is not a relic brought back to life but a new chapter in an old story, written by people who decided the story was worth continuing.

stimulus.title: Social Science: Keeping a Language Alive
stimulus.text:
When linguists speak of a language as endangered, they rarely mean that its words are disappearing from dictionaries. Dictionaries, after all, can preserve a language indefinitely, in the way a museum preserves a fossil. What linguists mean is that fewer and fewer children are learning it at home. A language can have tens of thousands of speakers and still be in danger if almost all of those speakers are grandparents; it can have only a few hundred and be relatively secure if those few hundred include toddlers. The crucial measure is not size but transmission: whether the language is being handed from one generation to the next.

Transmission tends to break down for reasons that have little to do with the language itself. When a family moves to a city, when schools teach in a single national language, when jobs and opportunity seem to require a different tongue, parents often make a reasonable calculation: their children will be better served by the language of power. Sometimes the calculation is forced on them. In many countries, children were punished in school for speaking their home language well into the twentieth century, and the shame attached to that punishment could last long after the policy ended.

Efforts to reverse this process, known as language revitalization, have multiplied in recent decades, and they have taught advocates some uncomfortable lessons. The first is that documentation, however valuable, is not the same as revival. Recording elderly speakers, compiling grammars, and archiving stories can preserve an extraordinary amount of knowledge, and these materials are often indispensable to later learners. But a language that exists only in recordings is, in an important sense, no longer being used to do anything: to argue, to joke, to comfort a child at night.

The second lesson is that classroom instruction alone rarely produces fluent speakers. A child who studies a heritage language for an hour a day, then spends the rest of the day in the dominant language, may learn a great deal about it without ever coming to think in it. For this reason, some of the most closely watched programs are immersion programs, in which young children spend the entire school day, and sometimes much of their home life, in the language being revived. The approach demands enormous resources: teachers who are fluent, materials that must often be written from scratch, and families willing to commit to it.

A third lesson concerns what counts as success. Revitalized languages almost always change. New learners, many of whom grew up speaking another language first, bring with them sounds, idioms, and patterns of grammar from that language. Elders sometimes find the speech of younger speakers jarring, even incorrect. Linguists who study these situations tend to be less troubled. Every living language changes, they point out, and a language spoken imperfectly by children is in a far stronger position than one spoken perfectly by no one.

This view is not universally shared, and the disagreement is not merely academic. For some communities, the purpose of revitalization is to recover a connection with ancestors, and a language that has drifted far from the speech of those ancestors may feel like a loss disguised as a gain. For others, the purpose is to give the language a future, and change is the price of that future. Both positions reflect real values, and the programs that seem to last are often those that make room for both, treating elders as the keepers of an authoritative tradition while allowing young speakers to make the language their own.

What revitalization cannot do is simply restore the past. A language that returns from the edge of disappearance returns into a different world from the one it left. That may be the most important lesson of all: a revived language is not a relic brought back to life but a new chapter in an old story, written by people who decided the story was worth continuing.

stimulus.title: Humanities: Saving Everyday Writing
stimulus.text:
When historians want to know what ordinary people thought and felt in the past, they often turn to letters. Official documents record what governments decided; newspapers record what editors judged worth printing. Letters record something more intimate: the worries of a farmer writing to a brother in the city, the excitement of a young woman describing her first train journey, the small jokes and complaints that make up most of a life.

The value of letters comes partly from their abundance. In the nineteenth century, cheap postage and rising literacy turned letter writing into a habit for millions of people, and families saved what they received. Letters were tied in ribbon, tucked into Bibles, packed into trunks that passed from one generation to the next. Many were lost, of course, but enough survived that archives today hold enormous collections written by people who never imagined anyone but the recipient would read them.

That lack of self-consciousness is precious. A writer who expects publication chooses words carefully and presents a polished self. A writer dashing off a note to a sister about a sick cow or a quarrel with a neighbor does neither. Spelling and grammar, too, can reveal where a writer grew up and how much schooling he or she received. Letters also preserve the texture of their moment in physical ways: the quality of the paper, the handwriting that grows shaky in old age, the stain of a coffee cup, the pressed flower that falls out when the envelope is opened.

I sometimes worry that future historians will have nothing comparable. People today write more than ever, but much of what they write is brief, scattered across many services, and easily deleted. No one ties a bundle of text messages in ribbon. Perhaps some of today's messages will survive by accident, as many old letters did. But accident is a poor archivist. When I imagine a historian a century from now trying to understand how an ordinary family lived in our time, I picture her searching for a trunk that no one thought to fill.
stimulus.text_b:
It is common to hear that our era will leave behind a “digital dark age,” a gap in the historical record caused by fragile files and forgotten passwords. The worry is understandable, and it is not baseless. Storage formats become obsolete, companies shut down their services, and data that is not actively maintained can become unreadable within a few decades. Anyone who has tried to open an old document created with software that no longer exists knows the feeling.

But the fear of a dark age often rests on a romantic picture of the past. The letters that survive from earlier centuries are not a representative sample of what people wrote. They are the ones that happened to be saved, disproportionately by literate, settled, relatively prosperous families with attics to store them in. Countless letters by the poor, the mobile, and the unlucky were burned, thrown out, or left to rot. The archive we inherited was shaped by chance and by privilege as much as by anyone's design.

The digital record, by contrast, is in danger of being too large rather than too small. Ordinary people now produce staggering quantities of writing, and much of it is stored, at least for a time, on servers that keep far more than any attic could hold. The challenge for archivists is not mainly that this material will vanish on its own but that no one will make deliberate decisions about what to keep, in what formats, and with what protections for the privacy of the people who wrote it.

Ordinary people now produce staggering quantities of writing, and much of it is stored, at least for a time, on servers that keep far more than any attic could hold. stimulus.text:

Studios sometimes distributed cue sheets suggesting appropriate pieces for each scene, such as a lively march for a parade or something mournful for a deathbed, and publishers sold thick anthologies of short, adaptable pieces sorted by mood. They watched the screen and made up music to fit it, shifting key and tempo as a chase gave way to a love scene or a storm broke over a ship at sea. A good accompanist could make an audience laugh at a pratfall a split second before it happened, or hold a room perfectly still.

Above all, he or she needed to watch the film as closely as any audience member while performing for that audience at the same time.
