stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: Night Ferry
stimulus.text:
The ferry left the mainland at eleven, and by the time it cleared the breakwater, Teo was the only passenger still on the open deck. The others had gone inside, where the benches were warm and a television bolted to the ceiling showed a game no one was watching. He preferred the cold. After nine months of dormitory radiators that clanked all night and a roommate who slept with the window shut, the wind off the strait felt like something he had been owed.

He had imagined this crossing many times during the spring, usually in the middle of an exam. In the imagined version he stood at the rail exactly as he was standing now, and the lights of the island rose out of the dark one by one, and he felt the whole year fall away from him like a coat he no longer needed. What he had not imagined was how small the lights would look. From the dormitory, the island had seemed enormous, the place where everything important had happened. From the deck, it looked like a handful of sparks someone had forgotten to put out.

“You're Ana Reyes's boy.” The voice came from behind him, and Teo turned to find a man in oil-stained coveralls leaning in the doorway of the engine room, wiping his hands on a rag that was dirtier than his hands. Teo recognized him vaguely, the way he recognized most adults on the island: as part of the scenery, like the church steeple or the tide charts posted outside the post office. “Hollis,” the man said. “I've run the engines on this boat since before you were born. Your mother used to ride out with her algebra homework. Never once finished it before we docked.”

Teo laughed, surprised. His mother taught math at the island's only school now, and the idea of her as a girl struggling with equations on a rolling deck seemed both impossible and entirely obvious. Hollis came to stand beside him at the rail. For a while neither of them spoke. The engines thudded beneath their feet with a steadiness Teo could feel in his teeth.

“So,” Hollis said eventually. “Is it what you expected? The mainland?” Teo started to give the answer he had been giving all year, on the phone to his parents and in messages to friends who had stayed behind: that it was great, that he was busy, that the library was open until two in the morning. But the dark made it easier to say something truer. “It's bigger,” he said. “Everyone there is from somewhere else, so nobody asks where you're from. I thought I'd like that more than I did.”

Hollis nodded as if this were information about the weather. “Your mother said the same thing, near enough, the first summer she came back.” He folded the rag into a neat square and tucked it into his pocket. “She said the trouble with leaving is that you change, and the trouble with coming back is that the island doesn't. Then she said she was wrong about the second part.”

“Wrong how?” Teo asked. Hollis shrugged. “Island changes, too. Just slower. Harbor's been dredged twice since you were little. The bakery's under new owners, and they put walnuts in everything now, which some people consider a crime. Old Mrs. Petrakis finally retired from the post office.” He paused. “Thing is, when you live here, you don't see it happening. You need to go away for a while before you can notice.”

The lights of the harbor had grown larger as they talked, and now Teo could pick out individual shapes: the floodlit fuel dock, the red blink of the channel marker, the square yellow windows of houses along the hill where people were still awake. One of those windows, he knew, was his own kitchen, where his mother would be sitting with a cup of tea she had let go cold, pretending not to wait for him.

Hollis pushed himself away from the rail. “Engines don't watch themselves,” he said, and disappeared below. Teo stayed where he was. The island was no longer a handful of sparks. It was not enormous, either. It was simply the size it was, and for the first time all year he thought he might be able to see it clearly.

stimulus.title: Humanities: Stitched Records
stimulus.text:
In the back room of a small county museum, a quilt lies folded in acid-free tissue, brought out only a few times a year. At first glance it is an ordinary object: a grid of fabric squares, faded in places, its stitches slightly uneven near one corner. But to the historians who study it, the quilt is something closer to a document. Each square was cut from clothing worn by members of a single farming family over roughly forty years. Read carefully, it records births, weddings, hard winters, and at least one year of unusual prosperity.

Historians have not always taken quilts seriously. For a long time, the objects that filled history books were the ones that powerful people left behind: letters, laws, ledgers, monuments. Women who worked at home, especially poor and rural women, rarely wrote memoirs or kept diaries that survived. Their lives were recorded instead in the things they made, and those things were often treated as decoration rather than evidence. A quilt might be admired for its colors and then put away, its story unasked. Historians who went looking for those women's lives often found that the written record simply went quiet.

That attitude began to change in the second half of the twentieth century, as historians grew more interested in ordinary lives and as museums began to collect everyday objects with new seriousness. Researchers discovered that quilts could answer questions that written records left blank. The fabrics in a quilt can often be dated by their dyes and printing methods, which changed over time in known ways. A sudden appearance of expensive imported cloth might signal a good harvest; a quilt pieced entirely from feed sacks might suggest a family stretching every resource.

The stitching itself can be revealing. Some quilts show the work of several different hands, with tight, regular stitches in one section and looser ones in another, suggesting that they were made collectively, perhaps at a gathering where neighbors worked side by side. Others contain names or initials embroidered into individual squares, a practice that turned a quilt into something like a signed petition or a guest book. In some communities, quilts were given to departing friends, each square contributed by a different person, so that the traveler carried a whole neighborhood along.

None of this means that a quilt can be read as simply as a letter. Its “language” is ambiguous, and historians must be careful not to invent stories that the evidence will not support. A dark square might mark a death in the family, or it might simply be the only fabric that was available that week. Popular legends have sometimes attached dramatic meanings to quilt patterns with little proof behind them. Responsible researchers combine what the quilt itself shows with other sources, such as census records, local newspapers, and family recollections, and acknowledge what remains uncertain.

For the families who made them, of course, most quilts were not meant to be evidence of anything. They were meant to keep people warm. That practical purpose is part of what makes them so valuable to historians now. Because quilts were made for use rather than for posterity, they capture the texture of daily life without the polish that people tend to apply when they know they are being recorded. A diary may be written for future readers; a blanket is written, so to speak, for a cold night.

The quilt in the county museum will probably never be used on a bed again. Visitors who come to see it are shown not only the pattern but a chart identifying, as nearly as researchers can tell, whose shirt or dress each square came from. Some squares are still labeled with a question mark. The museum's curators have decided to leave those question marks in place, on the principle that an honest gap in a record is better than a confident guess.

stimulus.title: Humanities: What Is an Old Building?
stimulus.text:
In the middle of the nineteenth century, many of Europe's great medieval churches were in poor condition. Centuries of weather, war, neglect, and well-meaning alteration had left them cracked, patched, and in some cases half-ruined. Some had been stripped of their sculpture during revolutions; others had been modernized in styles that clashed with their original design. Out of the effort to save them came one of the most enduring arguments in the history of architecture, an argument not about how to repair old buildings, exactly, but about what it means for an old building to be authentic.

On one side stood the French architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who oversaw the restoration of a number of France's most famous medieval buildings. Viollet-le-Duc was a brilliant scholar of Gothic construction, and his ambition was correspondingly large. To restore a building, he wrote, is not to maintain it or repair it but to reestablish it in a finished state that may never have existed at any given moment. Where a church had been left incomplete, or altered by later builders, he was willing to design and build what he believed its original makers would have built, had they been able.

On the other side stood the English critic John Ruskin, for whom this approach was not merely mistaken but destructive. Restoration, Ruskin argued, was “the most total destruction which a building can suffer,” because it replaced the actual marks of the original builders, including their particular chisel strokes, their irregularities, and the wear of centuries, with a modern imitation. The value of an old building lay precisely in its age and in the labor of the specific people who made it. A restored church might look more complete, but it would be, in his view, a kind of lie. Better to protect a building with careful maintenance, Ruskin urged, and when it could no longer stand, to let it fall.

It is tempting to cast this disagreement as a contest between boldness and caution, or between imagination and respect. But both men loved medieval architecture deeply, and both believed they were honoring it. Their difference lay in where they located a building's value. For Viollet-le-Duc, value resided in the design, the idea of the building, which a skilled architect could understand and complete. For Ruskin, value resided in the physical object itself, in the irreplaceable material history that no design could reproduce.

The practical consequences of these views can still be seen. Some buildings restored in the nineteenth century carry towers, spires, and ornaments that are, in effect, Victorian-era additions dressed in medieval style. Many visitors cannot tell the difference, and some of these additions have become beloved in their own right; several cities have had to decide whether a celebrated nineteenth-century addition is now old enough to deserve protection itself. Meanwhile, the movement Ruskin helped inspire, which favored repair over reinvention, shaped the conservation principles adopted in the following century, many of which call for new work to be clearly distinguishable from old.

Yet neither position escapes difficulty when applied strictly. Ruskin's approach, followed to its logical end, would allow much of the world's architectural heritage to crumble rather than be touched. Viollet-le-Duc's approach, followed to its logical end, would allow a confident architect to replace history with his own theory of it. Even the decision to do nothing is a decision, with consequences that someone must answer for. Most conservators today work somewhere between these poles, making case-by-case judgments about when a missing element should be rebuilt and when an absence should simply be respected.

The debate endures because the question at its center has no final answer. When we stand in front of an old building, are we looking at an idea that happens to be made of stone, or at stone that happens to carry an idea? Each generation of architects answers a little differently, and each answer leaves its own marks, which future generations, in turn, will have to decide whether to keep.

stimulus.title: Social Science: When Should School Start?
stimulus.text:
Ask a teenager to fall asleep at nine o'clock at night and you are likely to be disappointed, not because of stubbornness, but because of biology. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later. The hormone that helps signal that it is time to sleep begins to be released later in the evening than it was in childhood, so many teenagers simply do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or after.

At the same time, teenagers still need a great deal of sleep; most experts recommend somewhere between eight and ten hours a night. A student who cannot fall asleep before eleven and must wake at six to catch an early bus is, night after night, falling short. Sleeping late on weekends can make up some of the difference, but it also pushes the internal clock even later, making Monday morning harder still. Over a school year, the shortfall adds up.

The consequences are not trivial. Sleep-deprived students have more trouble paying attention, remembering what they learned, and controlling their moods. They are more likely to doze off in class and, for those old enough to drive, more likely to be involved in car accidents. Grades, too, can suffer when students arrive at their first class too tired to think clearly. Some research has linked chronic sleep loss in adolescence to higher rates of depression.

For these reasons, several major medical organizations have recommended that middle and high schools begin classes no earlier than 8:30 in the morning. Districts that have made the change have generally reported that students sleep longer on school nights, and some have reported better attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class. The change does not ask teenagers to become different people. It simply asks schools to fit the day to the students they actually have.

Adults sometimes respond that teenagers would sleep more if they put away their phones. Screens do make the problem worse, and good habits matter. But no amount of discipline will move a teenager's internal clock back to where it was at age ten.
stimulus.text_b:
I have read the research on adolescent sleep, and I do not dispute it. When our district's school board asked me to study whether we should move the high school's start time later, I expected the hardest part would be persuading skeptics of the science. Instead, the science turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was the buses.

Like many districts, ours uses the same fleet of buses and the same drivers for several routes each morning. The high school route runs first, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. Pushing the high school later would mean either hiring more drivers, who are already difficult to find, or pushing the younger children's start times earlier, which would put eight-year-olds at bus stops in the dark. Our transportation office estimated that even the cheapest workable plan would require several new routes. Neither option is free, and neither is simple.

Then there are the afternoons. A later start means a later dismissal. Our athletic teams already travel to games at schools with earlier schedules, and students would miss more class time to get there. Students with after-school jobs, many of whom help support their families, told us that a later dismissal could cost them hours of work. Parents who rely on older siblings to watch younger ones after school raised similar concerns.

I do not offer these complications as reasons to do nothing. Several neighboring districts have made the change, and their experiences suggest that many of the problems can be solved with time and money. Some found ways to arrange their routes more efficiently; others raised taxes to pay for additional drivers. My point is that a start time is not a single decision. It is connected to transportation budgets, labor markets, sports schedules, and family routines, and a change that looks obvious on paper can shift costs onto the people least able to absorb them.

stimulus.title: Social Science: When Should School Start?

During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later. The hormone that helps signal that it is time to sleep begins to be released later in the evening than it was in childhood, so many teenagers simply do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or after.

At the same time, teenagers still need a great deal of sleep; most experts recommend somewhere between eight and ten hours a night. A student who cannot fall asleep before eleven and must wake at six to catch an early bus is, night after night, falling short. Sleeping late on weekends can make up some of the difference, but it also pushes the internal clock even later, making Monday morning harder still. Over a school year, the shortfall adds up.

They are more likely to doze off in class and, for those old enough to drive, more likely to be involved in car accidents. When our district's school board asked me to study whether we should move the high school's start time later, I expected the hardest part would be persuading skeptics of the science. Instead, the science turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was the buses.

Like many districts, ours uses the same fleet of buses and the same drivers for several routes each morning. The high school route runs first, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. Pushing the high school later would mean either hiring more drivers, who are already difficult to find, or pushing the younger children's start times earlier, which would put eight-year-olds at bus stops in the dark. Our transportation office estimated that even the cheapest workable plan would require several new routes. Neither option is free, and neither is simple.

Then there are the afternoons. A later start means a later dismissal. Our athletic teams already travel to games at schools with earlier schedules, and students would miss more class time to get there. Students with after-school jobs, many of whom help support their families, told us that a later dismissal could cost them hours of work. Parents who rely on older siblings to watch younger ones after school raised similar concerns.

I do not offer these complications as reasons to do nothing. Several neighboring districts have made the change, and their experiences suggest that many of the problems can be solved with time and money. Some found ways to arrange their routes more efficiently; others raised taxes to pay for additional drivers. My point is that a start time is not a single decision. It is connected to transportation budgets, labor markets, sports schedules, and family routines, and a change that looks obvious on paper can shift costs onto the people least able to absorb them.

Our board is still deciding. Whatever it chooses, I hope it chooses with all of those people in view.

stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: The Ledger
stimulus.text:
On the last Saturday in August, my grandfather turned the sign on the door of Okafor Cycle Repair from OPEN to CLOSED for the final time. Then, because he could not help himself, he turned it back. “Someone might have a flat,” he said, as though the whole town had spent forty-one years waiting for this particular afternoon to need him. I was fifteen, and I had come to help him pack, which mostly meant wrapping wrenches in newspaper while he told me where each one had come from.

The shop was narrower than our kitchen at home and smelled of rubber and oil and the peppermints he kept in a coffee can by the register. Inner tubes hung from the ceiling like gray streamers. Along the back wall, under a calendar that had stopped at March of some year before I was born, stood the workbench, its surface so scarred by tools that it looked less like wood than like a map of rivers. I had spent whole summers on the stool beside that bench, handing him spokes and pretending to understand what he meant when he said a wheel was “almost true.”

By three o'clock most of the shelves were empty, and I found the ledger. It was wedged behind the drawer of the register, a green clothbound book with a broken spine, and when I pulled it out a few loose receipts fluttered to the floor. Inside, in my grandfather's slanted capitals, were names, dates, and repairs: NEW CHAIN, TWO TUBES, REBUILT BRAKES. Beside most entries he had written PAID and the date. But beside many others, more than I could count at a glance, there was only a small penciled circle.

“What do the circles mean?” I asked. He was on a ladder, unhooking the last of the inner tubes, and he did not turn around right away. “They mean the bike went home,” he said finally. I told him that every bike went home; that was the point of fixing them. He came down the ladder slowly, one rung at a time, the way he did everything now, and took the book from me. He ran his thumb down a page as if he were reading the names with his hand rather than his eyes.

“This one,” he said, tapping a circle, “was a boy who delivered newspapers. His chain broke on a Monday, and if he could not deliver on Tuesday he would lose the route. This one was a nurse who rode to the hospital at night because the buses stopped running at ten. This one I do not remember at all.” He smiled at that. “Maybe he was just a man with a bicycle and no money that week. That happens to people, too.”

I did the arithmetic in my head, the way my mother had taught me to do at the grocery store, and it came to a lot. Not a fortune, maybe, but enough that I thought of the summer he had sold his car, and of the winter he had kept the shop's heat turned so low that he worked in his coat. I wanted to be angry on his behalf. I wanted to find the newspaper boy, who would be a grown man now, and present him with a bill.

Instead I asked whether he had ever been tempted to collect. My grandfather considered the question with the seriousness he gave to bent wheels. “A bill is a kind of door,” he said. “Some people, when you hand it to them, they walk through it and never come back. I would rather they came back.” He closed the ledger and set it on top of the box marked KEEP, not the one marked RECYCLING, though there was no longer any business for it to record.

Near five o'clock the bell over the door rang. A woman about my mother's age stood in the doorway holding a child's bicycle with a flat front tire, and she looked embarrassed to find the shelves bare. “I heard you were closing,” she said. “I wasn't sure.” My grandfather was already reaching for the one pump we had not packed. I watched him kneel beside the little wheel, and I understood, without anyone explaining it to me, why he had turned the sign back around.

stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: The Translator
stimulus.text:
For most of my childhood I was my father's voice in English, a job no one assigned me and that I could not have described if anyone had asked. It began, as far as I can reconstruct, at the counter of a pharmacy when I was seven. My father had a prescription in one hand and a dictionary in the other, and the pharmacist, a patient man with a gray mustache, kept repeating a question about allergies more slowly and more loudly, as though volume were a kind of translation. I said the word in our language. My father answered. I said his answer in English. The pharmacist looked at me with an expression I would come to know well: relief mixed with a faint discomfort, as if he had been rescued by someone too small to be holding the rope.

After that, I was summoned to banks, to the landlord's office, to parent-teacher conferences at which I translated my own report card. I became expert in a vocabulary no other child in my class possessed: escrow, deductible, premium, lien. I learned that adults say the most important thing last, after a great deal of preamble, and that if you translate too quickly you miss it. I also learned, though I would not have put it this way, that the person who carries the words between two people holds a small and unofficial power. When the landlord said something cruel, I could soften it. When my father said something proud, I could make it sound polite.

I used that power more often than I like to admit. I told my father the bank teller had been “very sorry” when she had not been sorry at all. I told my teacher my father was “very busy at work” when he was, in fact, too embarrassed to sit in a classroom and be spoken to through his daughter. These were not lies, exactly, or they were the kind of lies that hold a roof up. I was protecting him, I believed, and protecting the strangers, too, from the friction of meeting each other without a cushion.

It took me many years, and in the end a single afternoon, to understand what the cushion had cost. I was nineteen and home from college, and my father needed to dispute a bill from the electric company. I had a summer job and could not come, and so for the first time in my memory he went alone. I spent the afternoon expecting a phone call that never arrived. When I got home he was at the kitchen table, the bill flattened under the sugar bowl, a new figure written beside the old one in his careful hand.

“How did you manage?” I asked, and I could hear in my own voice something I did not like, a note of surprise that was close to condescension. He looked at me for a long moment. “I talked,” he said. “She talked. It was slow. Twice we had to start again.” Then he added, in English, with an accent I had spent years trying to make invisible on his behalf: “She was nice to me. To me, not to you.”

I have thought about that sentence more than almost anything anyone has ever said to me. For years I had imagined that I was building a bridge between my father and the English-speaking world. It had not occurred to me that a bridge can also be a wall, that by standing in the middle of every conversation, I had made sure no one ever spoke to him directly. The clerk at the electric company had not been kinder than the clerks I remembered. She had simply been talking to the person in front of her, and for the first time, that person was him.

I do not regret the years of translating; I am not sure we would have managed without them. But I no longer think of them as purely a gift I gave. They were also something I took, a little at a time, without either of us noticing: the chance for my father to be clumsy, and patient, and understood on his own terms.

stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: The Translator
stimulus.text:
For most of my childhood I was my father's voice in English, a job no one assigned me and that I could not have described if anyone had asked. It began, as far as I can reconstruct, at the counter of a pharmacy when I was seven. My father had a prescription in one hand and a dictionary in the other, and the pharmacist, a patient man with a gray mustache, kept repeating a question about allergies more slowly and more loudly, as though volume were a kind of translation. I said the word in our language. My father answered. I said his answer in English. The pharmacist looked at me with an expression I would come to know well: relief mixed with a faint discomfort, as if he had been rescued by someone too small to be holding the rope.

After that, I was summoned to banks, to the landlord's office, to parent-teacher conferences at which I translated my own report card. I became expert in a vocabulary no other child in my class possessed: escrow, deductible, premium, lien. I learned that adults say the most important thing last, after a great deal of preamble, and that if you translate too quickly you miss it. I also learned, though I would not have put it this way, that the person who carries the words between two people holds a small and unofficial power. When the landlord said something cruel, I could soften it. When my father said something proud, I could make it sound polite.

I used that power more often than I like to admit. I told my father the bank teller had been “very sorry” when she had not been sorry at all. I told my teacher my father was “very busy at work” when he was, in fact, too embarrassed to sit in a classroom and be spoken to through his daughter. These were not lies, exactly, or they were the kind of lies that hold a roof up. I was protecting him, I believed, and protecting the strangers, too, from the friction of meeting each other without a cushion.

It took me many years, and in the end a single afternoon, to understand what the cushion had cost. I was nineteen and home from college, and my father needed to dispute a bill from the electric company. I had a summer job and could not come, and so for the first time in my memory he went alone. I spent the afternoon expecting a phone call that never arrived. When I got home he was at the kitchen table, the bill flattened under the sugar bowl, a new figure written beside the old one in his careful hand.

“How did you manage?” I asked, and I could hear in my own voice something I did not like, a note of surprise that was close to condescension. He looked at me for a long moment. “I talked,” he said. “She talked. It was slow. Twice we had to start again.” Then he added, in English, with an accent I had spent years trying to make invisible on his behalf: “She was nice to me. To me, not to you.”

I have thought about that sentence more than almost anything anyone has ever said to me. For years I had imagined that I was building a bridge between my father and the English-speaking world. It had not occurred to me that a bridge can also be a wall, that by standing in the middle of every conversation, I had made sure no one ever spoke to him directly. The clerk at the electric company had not been kinder than the clerks I remembered. She had simply been talking to the person in front of her, and for the first time, that person was him.

I do not regret the years of translating; I am not sure we would have managed without them. But I no longer think of them as purely a gift I gave. They were also something I took, a little at a time, without either of us noticing: the chance for my father to be clumsy, and patient, and understood on his own terms.

stimulus.title: Social Science: The Value of Effort
stimulus.text:
Anyone who has spent an evening assembling a bookcase from a flat box knows the peculiar pride that follows. The shelves may lean slightly; there may be a mysterious screw left over. Yet the finished piece feels more valuable than an identical bookcase delivered fully built. Behavioral researchers have given this feeling a name, sometimes calling it the “IKEA effect” after the furniture company famous for selling products that customers put together themselves, and they have spent a good deal of effort trying to understand it.

In a typical experiment, participants are asked to build something simple: a storage box, a folded paper animal, a small set of plastic bricks. Afterward, they are asked how much they would pay for their own creation. Other participants, who did not build anything, are asked to price the same objects. Again and again, builders place a higher value on their own work than non-builders do. In some versions of the study, builders priced their own lopsided creations at nearly the same level as versions made by skilled hobbyists. The effect appears even when the builders' results are noticeably clumsy.

Why should labor make an object seem more valuable? One explanation draws on an older idea in psychology called effort justification. People tend to dislike believing that they have wasted their time or energy. When we work hard for something, we resolve that discomfort, often without realizing it, by deciding that the thing must have been worth the work. The more we invest, the more we need the investment to have been wise. Psychologists have observed related patterns elsewhere: people who endure a difficult initiation to join a group, for instance, often report liking the group more than those who joined easily.

A second explanation focuses on competence. Completing a task, even a small one, is a demonstration to ourselves that we are capable. The finished object becomes a kind of trophy, a physical reminder of a skill successfully exercised. Consistent with this view, the effect seems to depend on actually finishing. In some studies, participants who built an object and then took it apart, or who were stopped before completing it, valued it no more highly than people who had never touched it.

Marketers noticed these findings quickly. Meal kits that arrive as a box of raw ingredients and a recipe card, toys that must be assembled before they can be played with, craft sets that leave the final steps to the buyer: all of these, whatever else they offer, give the customer a small role in production. Some historians of advertising have suggested that early instant cake mixes sold better once the recipe was changed to require a fresh egg, though the story is often told more neatly than the evidence supports. Either way, the customer does a little of the work and, in exchange, may feel a little more attached to the result.

But the same tendency that makes a homemade bookcase feel special can also lead people astray. Managers sometimes overvalue projects they designed themselves and continue funding them long after the evidence suggests they should stop. Writers may be reluctant to cut a paragraph that took hours to draft, even when it weakens the piece. Because the value we assign to our work is partly a reflection of the effort we spent, our judgments about that work are not entirely about the work itself. Homeowners who renovate a house themselves may likewise expect buyers to pay for the hours they spent, not just for the result.

None of this means that pride in one's own labor is foolish. The satisfaction of making something, and the attachment that follows, are among the ordinary pleasures of being human, and they may encourage people to learn skills and take care of what they own. The point is narrower: when we evaluate something we have built, we are not neutral judges. Knowing that can help us enjoy the crooked bookcase while still noticing that it leans.

stimulus.title: Natural Science: The Wandering Stones
stimulus.text:
Scattered across the farm fields and forests of northern Europe and North America lie boulders that do not belong where they are. Some are the size of a car; a few are as large as a house. Many are made of a type of rock entirely different from the bedrock beneath them, such as granite resting on limestone, and some can be traced to outcrops hundreds of kilometers away. For centuries, these misplaced stones posed a puzzle. Something had moved them, and whatever it was had been powerful enough to carry enormous weights across great distances.

Geologists call such boulders erratics, from a Latin word meaning “to wander.” In the early nineteenth century, the most widely accepted explanation for them was a vast flood. According to this view, a great deluge had swept across the continents, and the boulders had been carried along by the rushing water or by icebergs floating on its surface. The flood theory had the advantage of explaining erratics in many places at once, and it fit comfortably with traditional accounts of the earth's history.

Yet the theory had problems. Moving water sorts the material it carries: it drops heavy stones first and carries fine sand and silt farther, leaving neat layers behind. The deposits found alongside many erratics were not sorted at all. Boulders, gravel, sand, and clay lay jumbled together, as if they had been dumped all at once by something that did not distinguish between large and small. In addition, the bedrock in many of these regions was marked by long, parallel scratches, all running in roughly the same direction, as though something heavy had been dragged across it.

The explanation that eventually prevailed came from observers who had spent time in the Alps. There, glaciers could be seen doing exactly what the flood theory struggled to explain. A glacier is a river of ice, and as it creeps downhill it plucks rocks from the land beneath and beside it, carries them along, and grinds them against the bedrock, leaving scratches. When the ice melts, it drops everything it carries in unsorted heaps. Alpine residents had long noticed boulders lying far below the current edges of glaciers and concluded that the ice had once reached much farther.

In the late 1830s, the Swiss-born naturalist Louis Agassiz took this reasoning to a dramatic conclusion. If glaciers in the Alps had once been larger, he argued, then perhaps ice had once covered vast areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including lands that are now temperate. The erratics of northern Europe and North America, the jumbled deposits, the scratched bedrock: all of these could be explained by sheets of ice far larger than any glacier then existing. The idea of an ice age met strong resistance at first. It required imagining a world dramatically different from the present one, and it challenged both the flood theory and the assumption that the earth's climate had always been roughly the same.

Over the following decades, however, evidence accumulated. Geologists mapped the scratches on bedrock and found that they formed consistent patterns radiating outward from a few centers, just as one would expect if great ice sheets had spread from those centers. They traced erratics back to their sources and found that the stones had moved in the directions the scratches indicated. By the end of the nineteenth century, the idea that large parts of the Northern Hemisphere had once been buried under ice was widely accepted.

Today, scientists understand that there was not one ice age but many cycles of glacial advance and retreat over the past few million years. The erratics are reminders of the most recent of these advances, which ended more than ten thousand years ago. Some have become local landmarks, given names and climbed by generations of children; others serve as fence corners in farmers' fields, their history unnoticed. They sit where the ice abandoned them, ordinary-looking stones that once forced people to imagine an entirely different world.

stimulus.title: Solubility and Temperature
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students heated 100 g of distilled water to a set temperature in a beaker and added the salt one gram at a time, stirring after each addition, until no more would dissolve. They recorded the total mass dissolved at each temperature.
Results (the mass of salt that dissolved): at 40 °C, 58 g; at 60 °C, 97 g; at 80 °C, 149 g; at 100 °C, 213 g.

choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each light intensity and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

choices.text: Allow the temperature of the water to vary freely from one trial to the next
choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

choices.text: Test fewer values of light intensity so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

questions.explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

stimulus.title: Light and Photosynthesis
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water and set a lamp at distances giving several light intensities. They counted the oxygen bubbles released in one minute at each intensity, repeating each count three times.
Results (the rate of photosynthesis): at 100 µmol/m²/s, 13.3 bubbles/min; at 200 µmol/m²/s, 18.2 bubbles/min; at 300 µmol/m²/s, 20.7 bubbles/min; at 400 µmol/m²/s, 22.3 bubbles/min; at 500 µmol/m²/s, 23.3 bubbles/min.

stimulus.title: Seed Soaking and Germination
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students soaked batches of 50 radish seeds in water for a set number of hours, then placed each batch on damp paper towels in a covered tray. After 5 days they counted the seeds that had sprouted and converted the count to a percent.
Results (the percent of seeds that sprouted): at 8 h, 62%; at 12 h, 68%; at 16 h, 52%; at 20 h, 32%; at 24 h, 23%.

stimulus.title: Catalyst and Reaction Time
stimulus.text:

stimulus.title: Acid Concentration and Titration
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed 25 mL of an acid solution of known concentration in a flask with a few drops of indicator and added base solution from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changed color. They recorded the volume of base added.
Results (the volume of base needed): at 0.1 mol/L, 22.1 mL; at 0.15 mol/L, 33.1 mL; at 0.2 mol/L, 44.1 mL; at 0.25 mol/L, 55.2 mL; at 0.3 mol/L, 66.2 mL.
